system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2191-01-17 15:46:00 to 2191-01-21 14:04:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old female with a history of type I diabetes, end-stage renal disease with prior kidney and pancreas transplants, and severe mitral regurgitation was admitted for worsening heart failure symptoms. She underwent elective coronary artery bypass grafting x3 and mechanical mitral valve replacement. The surgery was performed due to severe three-vessel coronary disease and ischemic mitral regurgitation. She tolerated the procedure well, was extubated on postoperative day one, and transitioned to the telemetry floor. Her renal function remained stable throughout admission, and she was managed on warfarin for mechanical valve anticoagulation. By discharge on postoperative day six, she was ambulating with assistance, pain was controlled with oral medications, and incisions were healing. She was discharged to an extended care facility for rehabilitation with detailed instructions on wound care, activity restrictions, and medication management.
problems: Acute kidney failure with lesion of tubular necrosis
Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery
Surgical operation with transplant of whole organ causing abnormal patient reaction, or later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of operation

radiology_notes.text:
CT CHEST, ___.

Comparison chest CT ___ and comparison chest x-ray of ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Volumetric, multidetector CT of the chest was performed without
intravenous or oral contrast.  Images are presented for display in the axial
plane at 5-mm and 1.25-mm collimation.  A series of multiplanar reformation
images were also submitted for review.

FINDINGS:  Large left pleural effusion is present, occupying nearly the
entirety of the left hemithorax with associated rightward shift of the
mediastinum, inversion of the left hemidiaphragm, and atelectasis of the left
upper and lower lobes with only a small amount of residual aerated lung within
the superior segment left lower lobe and apex of the left upper lobe. 
Hounsfield units of the pleural effusion are slightly greater than simple
fluid, measuring about 20 Hounsfield units.  On the right, a small dependent
pleural effusion has decreased in size from the prior CT and has Hounsfield
units consistent with simple fluid, approximately 2.  The patient is status
post median sternotomy and mitral valve surgery.  Pericardial effusion is
small to moderate in size and new from the preoperative CT of ___.  Heart is mildly enlarged and diffuse coronary artery calcifications are
again visualized.  Small round fluid collection in the right anterior
mediastinum measuring 1.6 cm is new from the preoperative CT and has a tubular
longitudinal configuration.  This is not fully characterized without
intravenous contrast but could potentially represent fluid within the track of
a previous mediastinal drain in this location based on comparison postop chest
x-ray of ___.  A vascular abnormality is less likely but cannot be
excluded without intravenous contrast administration.

Within the aerated portions of the lungs, bilateral pattern of pulmonary edema
has resolved in the interval.

Exam was not specifically tailored to evaluate the subdiaphragmatic region,
but note is made of atrophy of the right kidney and diffuse vascular
calcifications throughout the abdominal aorta and its branches including the
renal arteries.  The left kidney is not imaged but was previously shown to be
atrophic.  Soft tissue structures are remarkable for mild anasarca.

Sternal wires appear intact.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Large left pleural effusion is similar to recent chest x-ray of ___ but substantially larger compared to earlier postoperative radiographs of
___.  Hounsfield units are slightly greater than simple fluid and could
reflect complicated contents including prior hemorrhage, but there is no
evidence to suggest active bleeding into the pleural space.  The effusion is
associated with marked inversion of left hemidiaphragm as well as shift of
mediastinal structures towards the right.

2.  Resolution of pulmonary edema and decrease in size of right pleural
effusion since ___ left chest CT.

INDICATION:  Right-sided thoracentesis, evaluate for pneumothorax.  Background
of coronary artery bypass grafting and mitral valve replacement.

COMPARISON:  Radiographs dating back to ___ and most recently ___.

FINDINGS:  A moderately large left pleural effusion has significantly
decreased in size since thoracentesis without evidence of pneumothorax.  There
is subtotal but adequate re-expansion of the left lower lobe.  Moderate
cardiomegaly is unchanged.  The appearance of the aortic valve replacement and
median sternotomy wires is satisfactory.  The right lung is normal in
appearance.  High density material opacifies the stomach and large bowel, this
may represent contrast.

IMPRESSION:  
1. No evidence of pneumothorax after thoracentesis.
2. Residual small-to-moderate left pleural effusion.

CHEST

HISTORY:  Shoulder pain.  Thoracentesis.

Two views.  Comparison with the previous study done ___.  There is
interval development of increased density in the lower left chest consistent
with parenchymal consolidation.  There are small bilateral pleural effusions
as well.  Interstitial markings have increased somewhat.  The left heart
border is obscured.  The patient is status post median sternotomy and MVR, as
demonstrated on the earlier exam.  Mediastinal structures appear unchanged.

IMPRESSION:  Interval development of consolidation in the lower left chest. 
Small bilateral pleural effusions.  Increased interstitial markings consistent
with development of mild edema.

INDICATION:  Persistent left pleural effusion.

___ and ___.

TWO VIEWS OF THE CHEST:  Note is made of cardiomegaly, which is unchanged. 
Also unchanged are multiple mediastinotomy wires and a mitral valve
prosthesis.  As before, there is a left pleural effusion, with expected
overlying subsegmental atelectasis.  The volume of this effusion is increased.
There is also suggestion of a tiny right pleural effusion, a finding which is
new from the comparison study.  Additionally, the degree of pulmonary edema
has progressed.  There is no pneumothorax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this stay. I see you came in because of shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been feeling more winded lately, especially when I walk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You were seen in clinic last week, and your exam showed decreased breath sounds on the left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the nurse said something about fluid in my lung. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we need to address. A chest X-ray showed a large pleural effusion on the left side — that’s fluid around the lung.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I remember now. They said they couldn’t do the procedure because of my blood thinner?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re on warfarin for your mechanical heart valve, and your INR was too high to safely remove the fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll admit you to reverse the blood thinner with vitamin K, then switch you to heparin. Once your INR is safe, we’ll drain the fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help me breathe better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, removing the fluid should improve your breathing. We also need to make sure it doesn’t come back quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My kidney numbers were off last time too — should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your kidney function closely. You have stage 4 chronic kidney disease, so we adjust medications carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes — I’ve been checking my sugars at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll manage your insulin here. Your type 1 diabetes is well-controlled, but we’ll keep an eye on it with your other conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just want to get back to feeling normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your INR came down after the vitamin K. We’re switching you to IV heparin now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can have the fluid drained today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the plan is to do a thoracentesis this morning. A small tube will remove the fluid from around your left lung.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get local numbing medicine. You might feel pressure, but not sharp pain. We’ll monitor your breathing and oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The thoracentesis went well. We removed about 1.2 liters of fluid from your left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wow, that much? Do you know what it was?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It wasn’t pure water — slightly denser, maybe from past bleeding or inflammation. We sent it for testing, but no infection seen so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe to be on heparin now with my transplanted kidney?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re using a low dose and monitoring closely. Your kidney function is stable for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m already breathing a little easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. A follow-up chest X-ray shows your lung has re-expanded well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed something new this morning. The chest X-ray shows some consolidation in your lower left lung.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Consolidation? Is that pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be. It might be from the lung re-expanding after the fluid was removed, or a mild infection. We’re not seeing fever or high white count.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be on antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting a low-risk antibiotic just in case. We don’t want to take chances with your heart and kidney history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My shoulder’s been aching too — is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Sometimes fluid or inflammation near the diaphragm can refer pain to the shoulder. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. But the latest chest X-ray shows the pleural effusion is starting to come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It suggests your heart failure might be contributing. You have chronic systolic heart failure, and that can cause fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So we need to adjust my heart meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re increasing your diuretic slightly to help your body get rid of extra fluid. We’ll watch your kidney function closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my INR — is it safe to go back on warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re restarting warfarin tomorrow. Once it’s therapeutic, we’ll stop the heparin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re ready to be discharged today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? I’m feeling much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your breathing has improved, your INR is in range, and you’re back on warfarin safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the fluid coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor that closely in clinic. It may require another drainage if it grows, but for now, the diuretic should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a cardiology and transplant clinic visit scheduled in three days. They’ll check your heart, kidney, and fluid status.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep taking your meds, watch your fluid intake, and call if you have trouble breathing again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And no penicillin — I remember my allergies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct — we’ve noted your allergies to penicillin and Percocet. You’ll get a full discharge summary with all instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ll make sure my primary doctor has a copy too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent idea. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old female with a history of type 1 diabetes, stage 4 chronic kidney disease, prior pancreas and kidney transplants, and recent mechanical mitral valve replacement was admitted for shortness of breath due to a large left pleural effusion. She had an elevated INR from warfarin, requiring reversal with vitamin K and bridging with heparin before a thoracentesis could be performed. The procedure was successfully completed, removing 1.2 liters of fluid, and her breathing improved. However, imaging showed reaccumulation of the effusion and new left lower lobe consolidation, prompting antibiotic treatment and diuretic adjustment for underlying heart failure. Her INR was stabilized, warfarin was restarted, and she was discharged with follow-up planned for ongoing management of heart failure, anticoagulation, and transplant-related complications.
